Minnesota’s medtech sector is a powerhouse—no doubt. But let’s cut through the applause: while innovators push boundaries, the Pentagon’s spending habits remain stuck in the Stone Age. The INNOVATE Act (S.853) funnels millions into SBIR/STTR programs, but D.C. still wastes billions propping up bloated defense contracts instead of fast-tracking breakthroughs.

Case in point: the Joint Autonomy Office’s $55M budget for “accelerating delivery” of systems while troops wait years for field-ready tech. Real readiness means slashing red tape, not rubber-stamping more bureaucracy.

Minnesota’s businesses deliver—Washington’s job is to get out of their way.

Rural healthcare shortages aren’t about funding—they’re about D.C. mismanagement. The FARM Act, Section 3, prioritizes retaining rural professionals, yet bureaucrats still funnel billions into bloated urban systems and foreign aid while Minnesota clinics scramble. Medical school debt? A crisis manufactured by D.C.’s refusal to audit predatory tuition hikes and pharma-backed residency quotas.

Instead of begging for more taxpayer cash, why not slash Medicaid’s administrative bloat (30% of its budget) and redirect those billions to loan forgiveness for docs who serve rural areas? Open Door’s struggle isn’t unique—it’s systemic.

Until Washington stops subsidizing corporate hospitals and starts enforcing merit-based incentives, rural Americans will keep paying the price for coastal elites’ neglect.

Fort Hood’s hearing protection upgrades are critical—hearing loss and tinnitus are top disability claims draining billions from veterans’ care. But let’s be real: why did it take this long? The DOD’s own 2024 Hearing Conservation Program update mandated fit-testing years after noise exposure risks were well-documented.

Starkey SoundGear’s involvement? Classic contractor reliance—innovative, sure, but at what markup? Taxpayers deserve transparency: what’s the per-unit cost versus bulk procurement?

Military readiness hinges on health, but bureaucratic inertia shouldn’t delay basic protections. Audit the supply chain—every dollar wasted on overpriced gear steals from frontline readiness.

Freeborn County’s ICE facility is a prime example of federal dysfunction—counties shouldn’t be stuck covering costs when D.C. fails to pay its bills. The facility budgeted $3M in ICE revenue for 2025, yet delays in federal reimbursements force local taxpayers to subsidize Washington’s incompetence. Medical expenses alone cost ICE $425K for inpatient mental healthcare in FY23, per DHS reports—yet bureaucrats still nickel-and-dime counties.

If Congress wants to “secure the border,” it needs to fully fund its own mandates instead of passing the buck to local governments. Accountability starts with paying what you owe.
